slides.say: Given: p, q and r are different positive integers, and r squared over p q is equal to p over q plus q over p. Which of the following is not necessarily true?

The equation looks complicated, so first we simplify it. Not necessarily true means it fails in at least one allowed case. So we're looking for the claim that can fail. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, by plugging in whole numbers that fit, and then with an insight, a right triangle, which shows why the other claims always hold.

[short pause] Let's simplify the right side. To add p over q and q over p, we need a common denominator, p times q. p over q is p squared over p q, and q over p is q squared over p q. So the right side is p squared plus q squared, over p q.
at: p over q is p squared over p q
and q over p is q squared

slides.say: Both sides now have the same denominator, p q, so their tops are equal. r squared equals p squared plus q squared.

[pause] Now let's plug in numbers. We need positive integers that fit r squared equals p squared plus q squared. The best-known ones are three, four and five, because nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. Here r is five.
at: r squared equals p squared plus q squared

slides.say: Choice number three says r is smaller than eight. With three, four and five it's true, but we need a case where it fails. Let's double all three numbers: six, eight and ten. Thirty-six plus sixty-four is a hundred, which is ten squared, so they fit too, and they're different positive integers. Now r is ten, and ten is not smaller than eight.
So choice number three fails in an allowed case. It's not necessarily true, and choice number three is our answer. One allowed case where it fails is all the question asks for, so we can stop here.
at: and choice number three is our

slides.say: [pause] Now the insight. Let's see why the other three claims always hold. r squared equals p squared plus q squared is Pythagoras. So p, q and r can be the sides of a right triangle, with legs p and q, and the longest side, r.
at: r squared equals p squared plus q squared is
can be the sides of a right triangle

slides.say: Choice number one says q is smaller than r, and choice number four says p is smaller than r. In a right triangle, the longest side is longer than each leg. So r is bigger than p and bigger than q, always. So choice numbers one and four always hold. With algebra it's the same idea: r squared is q squared plus a positive number, and all the numbers are positive, so r is bigger than q.
at: So r is bigger than p

slides.say: Choice number two says r is smaller than p plus q. And in any triangle, two sides together are longer than the third side. So p plus q is bigger than r, always. That's choice number two.
at: So p plus q is bigger

slides.say: But nothing in the triangle limits how long r is. So only choice number three can fail. Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: So only choice number three can fail
